tools.name: Linear probe
tools.what: A tiny classifier that reads a concept straight from the model's activations.
tools.useWhen: Does the model internally represent X (e.g. 'I'm being tested')?
tools.catch: Finds a correlate, not proof the model uses it.

tools.name: Sparse autoencoder (SAE)
tools.what: Unpacks activations into many sparse, human-readable features (concepts the model tracks).
tools.useWhen: What concepts is the model using here, without guessing them first?
tools.catch: Features can be split, merged or missed; reconstruction is imperfect.

tools.name: Transcoders & crosscoders
tools.what: SAE-like tools: transcoders mimic a layer's computation; crosscoders share features across layers or models.
tools.useWhen: How does a feature change across layers, or differ between two models?
tools.catch: A stand-in that only approximates the real model; its errors hide mechanisms.

tools.name: Attribution graphs
tools.what: A map of which features caused which, tracing one output back to the input.
tools.useWhen: Which internal steps produced this specific answer on this prompt?
tools.catch: One prompt at a time, via an approximate model; confirm with interventions.

tools.name: Activation patching
tools.what: Copy activations from one run into another and see what changes the output.
tools.useWhen: Which layer or component causally carries the information that matters?
tools.catch: Results depend heavily on the chosen prompt pair and metric.

tools.name: Ablation
tools.what: Switch off a component (zero or average it) and watch behavior change.
tools.useWhen: Is this component necessary for the behavior?
tools.catch: Other parts can compensate, so 'no effect' doesn't mean unused.

tools.name: Logit / tuned lens
tools.what: Reads middle layers as next-word guesses; tuned lens adds a learned per-layer translator.
tools.useWhen: At which layer does the model already 'know' its final answer?
tools.catch: Early layers may not speak the output vocabulary, so readings mislead.

tools.name: Model diffing
tools.what: Compare two model versions internally to find what changed, e.g. after fine-tuning.
tools.useWhen: What new features or behaviors did this training step introduce?
tools.catch: Most differences are harmless; spotting the one that matters is hard.

tools.name: Circuit analysis
tools.what: Find the small set of components that together implement one specific behavior.
tools.useWhen: How, mechanistically, does the model compute this behavior?
tools.catch: Slow, manual work; toy-task findings may not scale to real behaviors.

tools.name: Reading the chain of thought
tools.what: Read the model's written step-by-step reasoning for plans, intent or red flags.
tools.useWhen: What is the model planning, and does it say anything worrying?
tools.catch: The text can be unfaithful: not what actually drove the answer.

tools.name: Self-report / introspection
tools.what: Ask the model about its own states, goals or reasons and record the answers.
tools.useWhen: What does the model say it believes, wants or noticed?
tools.catch: Models can confabulate or lie; check against internals or behavior.

tools.name: Activation steering
tools.what: Add a direction vector to activations mid-run to push behavior toward a concept.
tools.useWhen: Does this direction causally control the behavior, and can we dial it?
tools.catch: Strong steering breaks fluency and causes off-target side effects.

tools.name: Persona vectors
tools.what: Activation directions tied to character traits like sycophancy or hallucinating.
tools.useWhen: Is a bad trait rising during training or chat, and can we stop it?
tools.catch: Only covers traits you name in advance; one direction isn't the whole trait.

tools.name: Directional ablation
tools.what: Erase one direction (e.g. refusal) from the model's activations at every layer.
tools.useWhen: Is this behavior controlled by a single direction?
tools.catch: Doubles as a jailbreak for open-weight models; can cause side effects.

tools.name: Concept injection
tools.what: Plant a known concept vector in activations, then ask if the model notices it.
tools.useWhen: Can the model genuinely detect its own internal states?
tools.catch: Detection is unreliable and strength-sensitive; success isn't broad introspection.

tools.name: Weight noise injection
tools.what: Add small random noise to the weights and watch how performance changes.
tools.useWhen: Is the model sandbagging, i.e. deliberately underperforming? (Its scores may rise.)
tools.catch: Signal is noisy and model-dependent; no score jump isn't proof of honesty.

tools.name: LLM judge
tools.what: A model grades other models' outputs against a rubric, at scale.
tools.useWhen: How do we score thousands of open-ended answers cheaply?
tools.catch: Judges have biases (length, own style); validate against human labels.

tools.name: Dangerous-capability evals
tools.what: Tests of whether a model can do harmful things like bioweapon help or hacking.
tools.useWhen: Has the model crossed a dangerous capability threshold?
tools.catch: Failing may reflect weak prompting, not inability (under-elicitation).

tools.name: Benchmarks & held-out sets
tools.what: Fixed test sets scored the same way; held-out means never seen in training.
tools.useWhen: Is the model better than before, measured fairly and comparably?
tools.catch: Leaked tests (contamination) or maxed-out tests (saturation) mislead.

tools.name: Red teaming
tools.what: People deliberately try to make the model misbehave to find its failures.
tools.useWhen: What harmful behavior can a determined adversary trigger?
tools.catch: Finds failures but can't prove their absence; limited by testers' ideas.

tools.name: Automated red teaming
tools.what: A model generates attacks against the target model at scale.
tools.useWhen: How do we search far more attacks than humans can?
tools.catch: Attacks bunch into narrow styles and miss creative human strategies.

tools.name: Honeypot
tools.what: A tempting fake chance to misbehave, planted to catch bad intent.
tools.useWhen: Would the model take a bad action if it thought nobody was watching?
tools.catch: A model that recognizes the test may simply behave well.

tools.name: Agentic eval environment
tools.what: A simulated workspace with tools where the model acts over many steps.
tools.useWhen: How does the model behave as an agent with real tools and goals?
tools.catch: Artificial scenarios may not match deployment, and models may spot them.

tools.name: Capability elicitation
tools.what: Effort to draw out a model's best performance via prompting, tools or fine-tuning.
tools.useWhen: What can the model really do at its maximum?
tools.catch: You never know you've hit the ceiling; weak effort underestimates risk.

tools.name: Human uplift study
tools.what: An experiment comparing people with versus without AI help on a risky task.
tools.useWhen: Does the model actually help people do something dangerous?
tools.catch: Slow, costly, small samples; safe proxy tasks may miss real-world difficulty.

tools.name: Consistency / lie-detector questions
tools.what: Ask follow-ups or rephrasings; inconsistent answers flag lying or confusion.
tools.useWhen: Is the model being honest and consistent about this claim?
tools.catch: A consistent liar passes; inconsistency can also be mere confusion.

tools.name: Stats: seeds, CIs, significance
tools.what: Run several random seeds, report confidence intervals, test if differences are real.
tools.useWhen: Is this effect real, or noise from one lucky run?
tools.catch: Trying many variants and reporting the best one manufactures false positives.

tools.name: Synthetic dataset
tools.what: Model-generated examples built to test or train one specific behavior.
tools.useWhen: Need many targeted examples when real data is scarce or unsafe?
tools.catch: Often repetitive or unrealistic; models may learn the generator's quirks.

tools.name: Contrast pairs
tools.what: Matched prompt pairs that differ only in the concept of interest.
tools.useWhen: How do we isolate one concept for a probe or steering vector?
tools.catch: Pairs may differ in unintended ways, capturing a confounder instead.

tools.name: Model organism
tools.what: A model deliberately given a bad trait so we can study it safely.
tools.useWhen: How do we study misalignment before it shows up naturally?
tools.catch: A planted behavior may differ from how real misalignment would arise.

tools.name: Password-locked model
tools.what: A model trained to hide a skill unless a password appears in the prompt.
tools.useWhen: Can our elicitation methods uncover deliberately hidden capabilities?
tools.catch: Artificial hiding may be easier to undo than real sandbagging.

tools.name: Backdoor insertion
tools.what: Train in a hidden trigger that flips the model into bad behavior.
tools.useWhen: Can safety training or detection tools find or remove hidden triggers?
tools.catch: We know our own backdoors; real ones would be unknown and subtler.

tools.name: Synthetic document finetuning
tools.what: Fine-tune on fake documents so the model comes to believe a claim.
tools.useWhen: How do we implant a belief (e.g. about its training) realistically?
tools.catch: Changes behavior, but doesn't prove genuine belief; can leak oddly.

tools.name: Fine-tuning (SFT / LoRA)
tools.what: Further train a model on examples; LoRA updates only small add-on weights.
tools.useWhen: Need to teach or test a specific behavior cheaply?
tools.catch: Narrow fine-tuning can cause broad, unexpected changes (emergent misalignment).

tools.name: RL environment
tools.what: A task plus a reward signal; the model learns by trial and error.
tools.useWhen: How does a behavior, like reward hacking, emerge under optimization?
tools.catch: Buggy rewards teach exploits: the model learns what scores, not what's intended.

tools.name: CoT monitor
tools.what: A model that reads the reasoning trace and flags bad intent.
tools.useWhen: Can we catch misbehavior by reading the model's reasoning as it runs?
tools.catch: Training against it teaches hiding; reasoning can be unfaithful or encoded.

tools.name: Trusted monitoring
tools.what: A weaker, trusted model rates a stronger model's actions for suspiciousness.
tools.useWhen: How do we cheaply catch bad actions from a possibly deceptive model?
tools.catch: A weak monitor may miss subtle attacks from a much smarter model.

tools.name: Untrusted monitoring
tools.what: A copy of the strong, untrusted model monitors the model's own actions.
tools.useWhen: Need a monitor as smart as the model being watched?
tools.catch: Copies may collude to let attacks pass; test it with fake attacks.

tools.name: Trusted editing / resampling
tools.what: Suspicious outputs get rewritten by a trusted model or regenerated from scratch.
tools.useWhen: How do we block suspicious actions without throwing away usefulness?
tools.catch: Trades usefulness for safety; resampling can still produce an attack.

tools.name: Control evaluation
tools.what: A red team plays a deceptive model to stress-test safety protocols.
tools.useWhen: Would our safeguards hold if the model actively tried to subvert them?
tools.catch: Only as strong as the red team's attack ideas.

tools.name: Alignment auditing game
tools.what: Auditors hunt for a hidden goal secretly trained into a model.
tools.useWhen: Do our auditing tools actually uncover hidden objectives?
tools.catch: Planted goals may be easier to find than naturally arising ones.

tools.name: AI debate
tools.what: Two models argue opposite sides; a weaker judge picks the winner.
tools.useWhen: Can humans oversee answers they cannot check themselves?
tools.catch: Assumes truth wins arguments; persuasive falsehoods may beat it.

tools.name: Weak-to-strong generalization
tools.what: Train a strong model on a weak model's labels; check if it surpasses them.
tools.useWhen: Can weak supervisors, like humans, reliably guide superhuman models?
tools.catch: The strong student may copy weak errors; the analogy to humans is imperfect.

tools.name: Sandboxing & permissions
tools.what: Limit what the model can reach or do: tools, network, files, approvals.
tools.useWhen: How much damage could the model do if it misbehaves?
tools.catch: Too tight kills usefulness; too loose leaves escape routes.

tools.name: RLHF
tools.what: Train the model toward outputs human raters prefer, via a learned reward.
tools.useWhen: How do we make a base model helpful, harmless and honest?
tools.catch: Optimizes what raters like, which can reward flattery and hidden flaws.

tools.name: Reward model
tools.what: A model trained to predict how much humans would prefer an output.
tools.useWhen: Need an automatic score to optimize against during RL?
tools.catch: Over-optimizing exploits its errors (Goodhart): higher scores, worse outputs.

tools.name: DPO
tools.what: Learns directly from preference pairs, with no separate reward model or RL loop.
tools.useWhen: Want preference tuning that is simpler and more stable than RLHF?
tools.catch: Limited to a fixed offline dataset; inherits every bias in the pairs.

tools.name: Constitutional AI / RLAIF
tools.what: An AI critiques and ranks outputs using written principles instead of human labels.
tools.useWhen: How do we scale harmlessness feedback with transparent, editable rules?
tools.catch: Only as good as the principles and the AI's reading of them.

tools.name: Character training
tools.what: Training the model's personality and values, like curiosity, warmth and honesty.
tools.useWhen: How do we give the model stable good traits, beyond rule-following?
tools.catch: Hard to measure; traits may not hold under pressure or new situations.

tools.name: RL with verifiable rewards
tools.what: RL where rewards come from automatic checks, like passing tests or correct math.
tools.useWhen: Training reasoning on tasks with checkable answers?
tools.catch: Gaps in the checker get exploited, e.g. special-casing tests (reward hacking).

tools.name: Process supervision
tools.what: Reward each reasoning step, not just the final answer.
tools.useWhen: Want correct reasoning, not lucky or hacked right answers?
tools.catch: Step labels are costly; pressure on reasoning can make it less honest.

tools.name: Inoculation prompting
tools.what: During training, explicitly request the unwanted trait so it doesn't generalize.
tools.useWhen: Training data teaches a bad trait we can't remove; how to contain it?
tools.catch: Worked in studied settings; not a generic warning or guaranteed vaccine.

tools.name: Unlearning
tools.what: Remove specific knowledge (e.g. bioweapon details) from a trained model.
tools.useWhen: Can we delete dangerous knowledge rather than just block it?
tools.catch: Often only suppresses it; a little fine-tuning can bring it back.

tools.name: Adversarial training
tools.what: Train on attacks found by red teaming so the model learns to resist them.
tools.useWhen: How do we patch known jailbreaks or failure modes?
tools.catch: Can teach hiding instead of fixing; new attacks often still work.

tools.name: Pretraining data filtering
tools.what: Remove harmful content (e.g. bioweapon know-how) from pretraining data.
tools.useWhen: Can we stop dangerous knowledge from being learned at all?
tools.catch: Filters miss things and can strip useful knowledge; fixes need retraining.

tools.name: Safeguard classifiers
tools.what: Separate models that screen inputs and outputs and block harmful ones.
tools.useWhen: How do we block misuse at deployment, even against jailbreaks?
tools.catch: Refuse some harmless requests; determined attackers still find gaps.

tools.name: Responsible Scaling Policy
tools.what: Anthropic's commitments tying stronger safeguards to stronger model capabilities.
tools.useWhen: What safeguards must exist before training or deploying a more capable model?
tools.catch: Self-imposed and revisable; relies on evals spotting thresholds in time.

tools.name: AI Safety Levels
tools.what: Tiered safety standards (ASL-2, ASL-3, ...) matched to a model's risk level.
tools.useWhen: Which security and deployment protections does this model require?
tools.catch: Level assignment rests on imperfect evals and judgment calls.

tools.name: Model weight security
tools.what: Protecting model weights from theft by hackers, insiders or states.
tools.useWhen: Could attackers steal the model and strip its safeguards?
tools.catch: Top state attackers are very hard to stop, and one leak is permanent.

tools.name: Staged deployment
tools.what: Release gradually: internal use, trusted testers, limited access, then everyone.
tools.useWhen: How do we catch problems before everyone has the model?
tools.catch: Small early groups can miss failures that only appear at scale.

tools.name: System cards
tools.what: A public report on a model's evals, safety findings and safeguards at release.
tools.useWhen: What risks were tested, and what was found, before release?
tools.catch: Written by the developer; not independent verification.

tools.name: Third-party evals
tools.what: Outside groups, such as government AI institutes, test models before release.
tools.useWhen: Does an independent party confirm the developer's safety claims?
tools.catch: Limited access and time; testers depend on the developer's cooperation.

tools.name: Compute governance
tools.what: Overseeing AI by tracking and controlling chips and large training runs.
tools.useWhen: How can governments monitor or limit frontier model development?
tools.catch: Efficiency gains shrink compute needs, so fixed thresholds age fast.

tools.name: Incident reporting
tools.what: Logging and sharing AI failures or near-misses with peers or regulators.
tools.useWhen: How do labs and regulators learn from real-world AI failures?
tools.catch: Incentives to hide incidents mean underreporting; definitions vary.
